qa.question:
According to the chairman's statement, as at the date of the annual report, the group had 
received booking fees for 63 residential units, of which 50 sale and purchase agreements 
(SPAs) had been completed, representing aggregate contracted sales of approximately $11.4 
million. A further nine residential units had been reserved, pending payment of the 
applicable booking fees. In addition, six commercial shophouses had been reserved for sale 
to the group's minority shareholders on an arm's-length basis. 
 
Note 19 of the financial statements reported revenue of $2.737 million from property 
development in Timor-Leste for FY2026. 
 
(Source: company annual report; emphasis added) 
 
The maiden recognition of revenue from the group's ongoing property development project 
in Timor-Leste was also identified as a key contributor to the improvement in the group's 
financial performance in FY2026. 
 
(i) 
Could management clarify how many residential units contributed to the 
$2.737 million of property development revenue recognised in FY2026? The 
63-unit sale figure mentioned in the chairman’s statement has a later cut-off at 
the date of the annual report. Is the booking fee 30% of the selling price?  
 
(ii) 
What were the achieved selling prices per square foot or square metre, and 
how did these compare with the selling prices assumed in the original 
feasibility study? 

(iii) 
Could management provide a breakdown of the buyer profile for the 63 
residential units, including the proportion of local and foreign buyers, 
individual purchasers and corporate entities?

Note 24 of the financial statements disclosed that, as at 31 July 2026, the group had $35.1 
million of contracted development expenditure that had not yet been provided for in the 
financial statements.  
 
 
(Source: company annual report) 
 
As at 31 July 2026, the group had cash and cash equivalents of $10.7 million. 
 
(i) 
How much has the group spent to date on the development of Timor Marina 
Square, and how much additional expenditure is required to complete the 
project? How does the remaining funding requirement compare with the 
group's available financial resources?  
 
During the year, it also obtained short-term working capital loans totalling approximately 
$13.4 million from Ma Jing, the daughter of the group's major shareholder, Mr Ma Weidong. 
The loans comprised $5.6 million carrying interest at 6% per annum and $7.84 million 
carrying interest at 3% per annum. 
 
(ii) 
How were the respective interest rates of 6% and 3% determined?   
 
On 18 June 2026, the company announced a proposed renounceable, non-underwritten 
rights issue of up to 268.3 million new ordinary shares at $0.10 per share, on the basis of one 
rights share for every existing share held. The proposed rights issue is expected to raise 
gross proceeds of approximately $26.53 million, before issue expenses. The net proceeds are 

intended to repay outstanding loans from a controlling shareholder and fund the group's 
ongoing property development in Timor-Leste. 
 
The previous rights issue in 2024 received valid acceptances for only 72.9% of the shares 
offered. 
 
(iii) 
What specific changes has the board made to address shareholders' 
concerns and improve participation in the proposed 1-for-1 rights issue? 
How will the company demonstrate that the proposed fundraising is 
supported by a credible business plan, realistic development milestones 
and an adequate expected return on shareholders' additional capital?

The company has announced that, as part of its board renewal process, Mr Loo Kenneth 
and Mr Sam Chong Keen will retire at the forthcoming AGM on 27 November 2026 and will 
not seek re-election. Mr Loo has served on the board for an aggregate period of nine years 
since his first appointment on 2 August 2017, while Mr Sam has served for more than 20 
years. 
 
In addition, Mr Darlington Tseng Te-Lin has informed the nominating committee and the 
board of his intention to step down as a non-executive and non-independent director at the 
2027 AGM, in support of the board's progressive renewal. 
 
Following the retirement of Mr Loo Kenneth and Mr Sam Chong Keen, only one independent 
director, Mr Lam Kwong Fai, will remain on the board. Consequently, the audit committee, 
nominating committee and remuneration committee will each fall below the minimum 
required membership of three directors. The company has indicated that it will endeavour 
to fill the vacancies within two months and, in any event, no later than three months. 
 
(i) 
What is the nominating committee's (NC's) board succession plan, and when 
did it commence the search for suitable candidates to fill the independent 
director positions? 

(Source: https://sg.finance.yahoo.com/quote/BQC.SI/) 
 
In 2016, there was a restructuring of the management team and an expansion of core 
businesses. 
 
(ii) 
What has been the total shareholder return over the past five and ten years 
(since the restructuring)?  
 
(iii) 
Has the NC undertaken a comprehensive review of the board's collective 
skills and competencies against the group's current strategic priorities and 
business risks? What material gaps, if any, have been identified? 
 
(iv) 
What specific criteria will the NC apply when selecting new independent 
directors, particularly in assessing their independence, relevant industry 
experience, financial and risk oversight capabilities, and ability to 
contribute effectively to the board and its committees?

globally, has the group assessed whether its existing intellectual property, 
audio technologies or engineering capabilities can be commercialised in 
these markets or any other growing sectors, including through licensing or 
partnerships? If so, which specific technologies have credible commercial 
applications, if any?

qa.question:
The group acquired investment properties totalling $20.17 million, marking a significant 
strategic shift following its exit from the TUMI business and the streamlining of its 
operations. The assets were part-funded by newly established bank borrowings, which 
amounted to $15.58 million as at 30 June 2026.  
 
The acquired properties comprise a commercial shop unit at 21 Tan Quee Lan, #01-03 and 
#01-03A, Singapore 188108, with a 999-year tenure, and a commercial shophouse at 10 
Bussorah Street, Singapore 199488, with a 99-year tenure commencing in December 2003. 
 
(i) 
What investment criteria and minimum return thresholds did the board 
apply when approving these acquisitions, including the expected rental 
yield and total return? Given that property investment represents a 
significant shift in the group’s business model, what relevant property 
investment and asset management expertise does the board and 
management possess?  
 
(ii) 
What specific competitive advantage does the group have in sourcing, 
managing or enhancing these assets?  
 
(iii) 
Are the properties generating positive cash flow to the group, after 
accounting for interest charges, overhead costs and fees, and how does the 
board assess whether the returns justify the capital committed? Given that 
these appear to be established commercial assets intended to generate 
rental income, where does management expect to create incremental value 
beyond collecting rent? 
 
Media reports1 have indicated that the company’s controlling shareholders have acquired a 
portfolio of freehold strata-titled rental units along Orchard Road.  
 
(iv) 
Given the potential overlap between the group’s property investment 
activities and the personal property interests of its controlling 
shareholders, how do the independent directors ensure that property 
investment opportunities are independently sourced and investment 
decisions are driven solely by the company’s commercial interests? What 
independent processes govern the identification, screening and selection of 
acquisition opportunities, and how does the board challenge management 
to ensure that assets are acquired or not acquired on their own investment 
merits?

Following the disposal of the TUMI business, completed on 1 April 2025, the group 
reported revenue of $21.1 million from Taiwan over a 12-month financial year ended 30 
June 2026. Management previously disclosed that the TUMI business had contributed

orchard-shopping-centre 

approximately 25% of revenue in the prior period. The group’s last reported 12-month 
financial year before FY2026 was FY2024, when revenue from Taiwan was $30.2 million. 
 
(i) 
What specific growth initiatives has management implemented to replace 
the revenue contribution from TUMI, and how much revenue have these 
initiatives generated to date? Which business segments or brands are 
expected to drive the group’s growth over the next two to three years? 
  
(ii) 
Within the group’s remaining brand portfolio, including Kangol, True 
Religion, Columbia and Sorel, which brands are the largest contributors to 
revenue and operating profit, and can management provide a breakdown 
by brand? 
 
The group’s headcount decreased from 273 employees as at 31 March 2024, when the TUMI 
business was still included, to 192 as at 30 June 2025 following the disposal. Headcount 
subsequently increased to 228 as at 30 June 2026, a rise of 18.8% year on year. 
 
(iii) 
What business activities or strategic initiatives account for this ~20% 
increase? Could management break down the increase by function and 
explain the expected contribution of these hires to the group’s growth plans? 
What key productivity metrics does management track, and how have these 
metrics changed following the disposal of TUMI?

Mr Goh Ching Wah, George, the group executive chairman, will retire by rotation and 
seek re-election at the forthcoming annual general meeting. Mr Goh Ching Huat, Steven is the 
chief executive officer and executive director, while Mr Goh Ching Lai, Joe is a non-executive 
director.  
 
(i) 
Could the board clarify the respective roles, responsibilities and decision-
making authority of the executive chairman and the CEO, including how 
their responsibilities are differentiated and any areas of overlap? Are both 
executive directors employed on a full-time basis, and do they devote their 
full working time to the group? 
 
The remuneration trend for the two executive directors over the past three financial 
reporting periods are summarised below, based on the company’s remuneration disclosure 
and SIAS’ calculations. 

(Compiled from company annual reports; emphasis added) 
 
Estimated base/fixed salary (FY2024 → FP2025^ → FY2026): 
 
Mr Goh Ching Wah: $156,000 → $246,000 → $723,000 
Mr Goh Ching Huat: $157,000 → $272,000 → $745,000  
 
^FP2025 covers a 15-month financial period. The figures above have been adjusted to a 12-
month equivalent for comparability.

company in June 2024, and again in May 2025. 
 
(ii) 
Can the remuneration committee (RC) confirm that the remuneration 
disclosures are accurate and that the executive directors’ base/fixed 
salaries have increased yearly, and by substantial amounts? What were the 
reasons for the increases given that the FY2026 base/fixed salary is almost 
5 times the FY2024 base/fixed salary? Were these salary increases 
documented in the directors’ service agreements or approved by the RC 
through separate remuneration decisions? Were the relevant terms and 
approvals in place before the increases took effect? 
 
In addition, in FY2026, the executive directors were each paid about $1.02 million and $1.04 
million respectively while the group recorded an operating loss of $(2.4) million.  
 
(iii) 
What performance criteria, benchmarks and weightings did the RC apply in 
determining their FY2026 remuneration, and how did the group’s operating 
performance affect the final remuneration outcomes? 
 
(iv) 
Given the group’s scaled-down operations following the disposal of the 
TUMI business and its operating loss in FY2026, how does the RC 
demonstrate that the executive directors’ remuneration, especially 
base/fixed salary, remains proportionate to the group’s current scale, 
financial performance and value creation (Principle 7 of the 2018 Code of 
Corporate Governance)?

qa.question:
For the financial year ended 31 December 2025, the group reported revenue of RM2.01 
million. According to management, the improvement was supported by higher quarry 
production and improving sales demand as operations progressed. The group also reported 
further development of the marble quarry, increased production output and expansion into 
the Middle Eastern market.  
 
(Source: company annual report) 
 
The group has been transitioning from its traditional ground calcium carbonate (GCC) 
operations towards marble quarrying, with repair works at the marble quarry 
recommencing more than six years ago since June 2020. 
 
(i) 
Can management provide a breakdown of FY2025 revenue between marble 
blocks and GCC? How has the revenue mix evolved over the past three 
financial years? 
 
(ii) 
How many quarry faces are currently in active production of marble blocks? 
What are the principal constraints on scaling production, including quarry 
development, equipment, labour, processing capacity, logistics or working 
capital? 
 
(iii) 
What progress has the group made in developing its Middle Eastern market, 
in terms of customer acquisition, confirmed orders, shipment volumes and 
revenue contribution? To what extent have the ongoing conflicts in the 
Middle East affected customer demand, order fulfilment, shipping, logistics 
costs or payment risk?

The group’s production projections for marble blocks have been materially reduced over 
successive annual reports. In the 2023 annual report, management projected annual 
production of 30,000 tonnes in FY2026. This was reduced to 15,000 tonnes in the 2024 

annual report and further to 750 tonnes in the 2025 annual report, representing a 97.5% 
reduction from the original projection. 
 
 
(Compiled from company annual reports)  
 
(i) 
What were the principal factors behind the successive downward revisions 
to the quarry’s production projections? To what extent were these 
attributable to technical or geological constraints, equipment and 
infrastructure limitations, operational execution, market demand or other 
factors? Which of the original assumptions relied upon in the board’s 
approval to enter the marble business have proved unrealistic?  
 
(ii) 
Given the scale of the revisions, what guidance and intervention has the 
board provided to management? How does the board monitor progress 
against production targets?  
 
(iii) 
In light of the substantial reduction in projected production, has the board 
reassessed the quarry’s commercial viability and the group’s original 
investment thesis? What minimum return thresholds and performance 
milestones must the quarry meet to justify further investment, and what 
specific conditions would trigger a decision to suspend additional capital 
expenditure or exit the project?

The board is of the opinion that the group is able to operate as a going concern1 and are 
able to meet their obligations as and when they fall due, and that the group’s working capital 
is sufficient to meet their present requirements for at least the next twelve months.  
 
1 As at 31 December 2025, the group’s and the company’s current liabilities exceeded its current assets by 
RM6.13 million (2024: RM12.47 million) and RM8.84 million (2024: RM7.08 million) respectively.  

This assessment is based, among other factors, on expected revenue from the sale of 
limestone and marble products to customers in South-East Asia, which the board expects to 
be sufficient to cover the group’s operating costs..  
 
(i) 
Given that the auditors have issued a disclaimer of opinion, can 
management provide shareholders with the revenue projections 
underpinning the board’s going-concern assessment, including the 
expected sales volumes, average selling prices and timing of revenue 
recognition for limestone and marble products? With approximately ten 
months of FY2026 elapsed, has the group achieved its projected revenue to 
date? 
 
(ii) 
Has management identified any non-core quarry land or underutilised 
equipment, such as crusher plants, that could be monetised to improve the 
group’s liquidity?  
 
As at 31 December 2025, the group reported total current liabilities of RM13.88 million, 
including lease liabilities, but held only RM89,651 in cash. 
 
 
The independent auditor has issued a disclaimer of opinion on the following bases: 
- 
the appropriateness of the going concern assumption; 
- 
the impairment assessment of the group’s property, plant and equipment; and 
- 
the impairment assessment of the company’s investments in subsidiaries and amounts due from 
subsidiaries. 

(Source: company annual report; emphasis added) 
 
(iii) 
Can management provide a breakdown of how these current liabilities are 
expected to be settled, particularly trade payables, other payables and 
accrued operating expenses? 
 
(iv) 
Has the board considered whether a rights issue would be a prudent and 
viable means of strengthening the group’s liquidity and balance sheet?
